/WEDNESDAY THROUGH MONDAY/...
Issued at 224 PM CDT Mon Sep 28 2026

(Wednesday - Friday)

Mostly dry weather is expected on Wednesday along with what should 
be the warmest day of the week. Temperatures at 850 hPa approach 
+18C, or above the 95th percentile of climatology. At least partial 
sunshine is also forecast, though there probably will be more clouds 
in northeast Missouri and west-central Illinois closer to the 
surface cold front. Highs may be closer to 80 degrees in these 
locations, but in the upper 80s to near 90 degrees for most of the 
rest of the area. While these values should fall several degrees 
short of daily records, they would be about 10-15 degrees above 
normal for the date and a fitting way to end what will be the 
warmest September on record at both KSTL and KCOU.

The chances of rain showers begin to increase on Wednesday in our 
far northern counties, but ramp up considerably late Wednesday night 
into Thursday as a slow-moving cold front begins to move through our 
region. The period of heaviest rainfall is likely to be on Thursday 
as a midlevel shortwave trough moves across the region. Strong, deep 
ascent is expected along the frontal zone, which should mean 
widespread showers along with a few embedded thunderstorms. The 
rainfall likely also will be pretty efficient given precipitable 
water values over 1.8" (>99th percentile of climatology) and very 
deep warm cloud depths (>12 kft AGL). The anomalous moisture is due 
at least in part to Hurricane Polo, as its remnants get captured by 
the anomalous troughing ejecting out of the desert southwest. 
Limited convection should be a deterrent to rainfall rates high 
enough to cause flash flooding, but river flooding is definitely 
possible. The northern part of the Mississippi and western portion 
of the Missouri rivers have the best chance (30-50%) of seeing 
flooding from this event, with even northern tributaries (i.e., 
Fabius rivers) all below 20% on the latest Hydrological Ensemble 
Forecasting Service (HEFS) outlooks. If the rainfall is heavier 
upstream than forecast, there is even a low chance (10-30%) for 
moderate flooding along these mainstem rivers. The cold front will 
continue to slowly move southeast through the area through Friday 
morning, but the mid/upper level forcing is considerably weaker late 
Thursday night into early Friday along/behind the boundary. 
Therefore, there should be a substantial gradient across the region 
in terms of rainfall totals. Probabilistic information from the LREF 
shows this gradient fairly well for chances for 1+" (70-40%) and 2+" 
(30-5%) from northwest to southeast. Even parts of southeast 
Missouri and southwest Illinois though do have about a 70% of seeing 
at least 0.50" of rain. This is where dry conditions have been for 
~6 weeks, and appreciable rainfall is needed most.

Temperature uncertainty increases on Thursday, as the exact frontal 
location and speed will be critical for afternoon highs. Ahead of 
the front, another day in the mid to possibly upper 80s are 
expected. Temperatures behind the front however will be 
significantly cooler, with upper 60s and low 70s most likely. The 
front should be southeast of the entire area by late Friday morning, 
so much cooler temperatures are expected areawide. Highs in the mid 
60s to mid 70s are forecast from northwest to southeast.


(Friday Night - Next Monday)

Seasonably cool temperatures along with mostly dry conditions are 
forecast for the weekend into early next week. There is increasing 
confidence that the front should push far enough south of the area 
to yield these dry conditions. There are some lingering chances for 
rain, mainly early this weekend across our southern counties, but 
these likely will continue to drop over the next 24-48 hours as 
uncertainty with the evolution of the front decreases. Confidence is 
pretty high that the front will make it well south of our area due 
to the strong (~1026 hPa; >90th percentile) surface high pushing 
southeastward out of the northern Plains this weekend. Climatology 
also favors cold fronts in early October to push at least into the 
mid south.
